chunks: "Serpentining is when you deliberately add squiggles to a trace to make it longer, so signals that start together also arrive together.
It matters for synchronisation because in a clocked bus, say a DDR byte lane, the receiver samples every data bit relative to the clock or strobe.
If one bit arrives 40 picoseconds later than the others, that eats directly into the setup and hold window.
The sums are simple: on FR-4 a signal moves at about 6 picoseconds per millimetre, so 6 mm of mismatch is about 35 picoseconds of skew. A 3.
2 Gb/s bit lasts 312 picoseconds; subtract setup, hold and jitter and you may only have around 100 picoseconds of window to spend on skew.
So I find the longest net in the group and add meanders to the others until they all match within the budget.

To do it properly, I keep the meander legs spaced at least three or four trace widths apart, otherwise the legs couple to each other and the signal partly takes a shortcut, so the effective delay is less than the length says.
I put the meander near the source of the mismatch, keep it away from vias and breakouts, and match in time, not millimetres, because stripline and microstrip have different speeds and vias add delay.
I also make sure I haven't broken the return path under it."
